name: Bianca Novak

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to employers, AI companies, unions, parties or government. What you say stays confidential. What does an ordinary workday look like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Most mornings I'm out of the South Road depot with a crew repairing overhead power lines. I check the isolation paperwork, test the wire, then take my turn in the bucket; the best bit is putting a dark street back on. The worst is pressure to hurry when a map or a manager says a line should be safe.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: And outside the depot, what are you balancing?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm 43, with a vocational certificate and apprenticeship behind me, and I know this work well enough to train an apprentice without pretending to know everything. My partner works bakery shifts, and our two children are in school; the mortgage and about three months of savings keep me careful. I'll use AI now and then to straighten a report, but I trust a meter and a second pair of eyes on a pole.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew the computer can tidy a work order, but it cannot tell us whether a line is safe to touch. Keep the apprenticeship solid and let the office have its small time saving.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be relieved, though our mortgage still takes a big bite each month. My linework and my partner's bakery shifts feel fairly steady, but our three-month cushion isn't a holiday fund.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll keep taking the overhead repair rota and check the isolation log myself before anyone climbs. From next pay, I'll move a little extra into the emergency account, perhaps the price of one family takeaway each week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly calm about my work, and still watchful about our bills. A quiet year would let me sleep without planning another trade.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to the apprentice on a routine repair?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At the depot I'd tell Niko, the apprentice, that a clean screen never proves a dead line. He has to test the conductor with me and show me the reading before he goes up. A clean screen never proves a dead power line; Niko, my apprentice, has to show me the test reading.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Where would the extra saving come from?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start with takeaway nights, not the children's school shoes. My partner's bakery hours can move around, so I want the account to cover four months before we loosen up.

say: **Work orders** may get neater, but our crew still tests each line before anyone touches it.
**Apprenticeship** should keep its place because a screen cannot certify a safe climb.
think: My **lineworker pay** seems secure in this picture, though our mortgage and variable bakery hours still matter.
Our **three-month cushion** makes a routine household setback more troubling than a little office automation.
do: **Keep** the overhead repair rota and personally check the isolation log before each climb.
**Save** the cost of one weekly takeaway from new pay until the household has four months of expenses.
feel: **Calm** about the linework, with a little watchfulness about household bills.
S0.quote: A clean screen never proves a dead power line; Niko, my apprentice, has to show me the test reading.
fieldNote: She puts **physical testing** ahead of any report, even in the mildest scenario.
Her **mortgage** and the bakery's variable shifts explain the small saving plan despite confidence in her own trade.

steps.text: Keep overhead repair rota and check isolation logs before climbs
Save one takeaway cost each week from new pay

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say planners can use software to draw a job faster, but the crew still has to make the pole and conductor safe. I'd ask who signs a plan when the ground looks different from the map.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The paperwork is a small part of my week, so I don't expect my place on the crew to vanish at once. If fewer planners come through the depot, though, I could end up carrying their checking work without more pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll ask our supervisor to put me on a pilot of the new route plans, then compare three jobs against what we find on site. In the first year I'll document wrong clearances and take the paid switching refresher if the company offers it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy fits better than frightened. I'd be angry if a cheaper plan pushed the risk onto the person up the pole.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens if a generated plan misses a clearance?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd mark the plan, stop the work and call dispatch before we touch anything. I'd rather explain an hour's delay than ask Niko to climb beside a line we haven't cleared. I'd rather explain an hour's delay than ask my apprentice to climb beside a line we haven't cleared.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you pay for that switching course yourself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want the company to pay for the refresher and give me time on shift. With two children and a mortgage, I won't buy a course merely because somebody says it might matter.

say: **Software plans** can save office time, provided the field crew can challenge what the map says.
**Safety sign-off** needs a named person when a generated route conflicts with the pole in front of us.
think: My **hands-on work** should last longer than the depot's planning posts, which are easier for AI to change.
I fear **extra checking** may land on our crew without the time or pay to do it properly.
do: **Compare** three generated route plans with actual pole clearances during a company pilot.
**Record** wrong clearances and take a company-funded switching refresher if a place opens.
feel: **Uneasy** about rushed plans and extra accountability, though I expect to keep working.
S1.quote: I'd rather explain an hour's delay than ask my apprentice to climb beside a line we haven't cleared.
fieldNote: She separates **office planning** from line repair and expects her own role to change more slowly.
The risk she names is **responsibility drift**: field crews checking faster plans under unchanged schedules.
Her course plan depends on **company funding** and time on shift.

steps.text: Compare three generated route plans against pole clearances on site
Take company-funded switching refresher if offered on shift

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the thinking system arriving in 2028 would remake dispatch before it remakes a storm crew. The capable robots around 2031 are when I'd really ask how many of us the electricity company means to keep.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years gives us too little time to pay the mortgage down or change trades. My partner's bakery accounts could be automated earlier, and three months of savings would go fast if her shifts were cut. My climbing certificate won't pay the mortgage if line-repair robots take half the crew.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This month I'll ask the bakery and my supervisor separately how they plan to staff through 2028. I'll stop the planned kitchen renovation, put that money into our emergency account, and ask about a company-paid course on testing robotic line repairs before 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm anxious, especially for the space between the first announcement and any real plan. I can still climb, but a family cannot live on skill alone if the work dries up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which household payment would you protect first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If bakery hours drop, we'll cancel the renovation and hold the cash for mortgage payments. I'd keep taking line repair shifts until the company gives a real answer on robot crews.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you switch employers before robots arrived?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I wouldn't leave my job on a rumour. I'd apply to nearby line crews if my company posts cuts, and I would only pay for a course once I know it leads to work.

say: **Dispatch** may change when thinking AI arrives in 2028; power-line robots around 2031 threaten crew numbers more directly.
**Staffing plans** from the company matter more to me than promises that new tools will create work.
think: My partner's **bakery hours** could shrink before my outdoor linework does, leaving our mortgage exposed.
Our **three-month savings** cannot cover a long gap if capable robots reduce field crews after 2031.
do: **Ask** both employers for their staffing plans through the first two years.
**Cancel** the kitchen renovation and save that planned spending for mortgage payments.
**Seek** a company-paid course on testing robotic line repairs before 2031.
feel: **Anxious** by the short runway and two possible losses of household income.
S2.quote: My climbing certificate won't pay the mortgage if line-repair robots take half the crew.
fieldNote: The **2028 thinking shift** touches her partner's bakery work sooner than her own climbing work.
She treats **2031 robots** as the main direct threat to lineworker staffing.
She pauses a planned renovation and seeks **employer-funded training**, with no firm offer yet.

steps.text: Cancel planned kitchen renovation and cut discretionary spending
Keep taking line repair shifts while awaiting the company crew plan
Apply to nearby line crews if the company posts field cuts

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to test machines properly, not enough to pretend the power company will keep every crew. Thinking AI in 2031 changes dispatch first, and robots around 2034 bring the harder argument.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 48 I could have a stronger mortgage position if we start now. I'd still expect robotic repair to reduce some crew hours, but a person may be needed to inspect the work and handle awkward sites; I cannot count on that post.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll ask for the company's training map at the next crew meeting and try its inspection tools only on supervised jobs. We'll add a fixed amount from each pay packet to the mortgage, and I'd apply for a field-inspection vacancy if those posts actually open.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, though less cornered than in the two-year picture. A few years lets our family prepare, but it also lets me watch a crew shrink slowly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you ask when a robot inspection trial starts?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask who authorises a robot to approach an energised line and who stops it when the test is odd. If nobody can answer, I'd refuse that job until the method is clear. I won't send a line-repair robot near an energised wire until somebody can name who stops it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Where would mortgage overpayments come from?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The extra payments come from postponing a new car, not from pretending the children need nothing. If my bakery-working partner loses hours first, we'd stop the mortgage overpayments and use the money for regular bills.

say: **Five years** permit proper trials and a staffing plan before robots reach line repair around 2034.
**Human sign-off** still matters whenever a robot approaches an energised line.
think: I could have **less mortgage debt** by 2034, but no inspection role is promised.
A slow **crew reduction** could cut my hours before any formal redundancy notice.
do: **Request** a training map at the next electricity company crew meeting.
**Try** inspection tools on supervised company jobs while recording failures.
**Overpay** the mortgage from the postponed car budget while both incomes hold.
feel: **Anxious** about declining crew hours, though the five-year runway gives us room to act.
S3.quote: I won't send a line-repair robot near an energised wire until somebody can name who stops it.
fieldNote: She sees **supervised trials** as proof of whether inspection work could remain for people.
Her **mortgage overpayments** depend on both incomes holding and a postponed car purchase.
She would halt a robot job over an unclear **stop procedure**, even with time to prepare.

steps.text: Keep line repair shifts while trialling supervised inspection tools
Overpay mortgage from postponed car budget while both incomes hold

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a decade is a real chance to teach younger crews both the old tests and the new equipment. Thinking AI in 2036 would still hit the office first; robots around 2039 would meet a different version of me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll be 56 when the robot date comes, so I could possibly finish my working years on inspections or training if such jobs are offered. I don't want to sell the children a promise about my job that the electricity company hasn't made.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll keep my certificate current and ask every year which safety and inspection roles the company is actually hiring for. We'll make modest extra mortgage payments while both pay packets come in, then review the family budget when the children finish school.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but I can picture a route through it. Ten years lets us pay debt and give the children choices without asking them to carry us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your daughter about her studies?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my daughter to choose her apprenticeship or study for the work she likes, not just to dodge a machine. We can help with fees only if the mortgage and emergency account are sound.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make an inspection role a real option?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A real offer would be a paid inspection or training place, with a clear qualification and wage. I won't call an occasional mentoring day a replacement for a full lineworker wage.

say: **Ten years** allow the electricity company to train crews before capable line-repair robots arrive around 2039.
**Apprentices** still need the old safety tests as well as any new equipment.
think: At **56**, I might move into inspection or training, but only if the company offers paid posts.
I want our **children's choices** to rest on a sound mortgage and emergency account, not guesses about robots.
do: **Renew** the linework certificate and ask annually about paid inspection openings.
**Overpay** the mortgage modestly while both household wages continue.
feel: **Uneasy** about future roles, with enough time to prepare carefully.
S4.quote: I won't call an occasional mentoring day a replacement for a full lineworker wage.
fieldNote: Her longer horizon changes the question from immediate survival to **paid later-career work**.
She declines to promise the children that **inspection posts** will exist.
The family's **mortgage plan** depends on both wages continuing.

steps.text: Renew linework certificate and check paid inspection openings annually
Overpay mortgage modestly while both household wages continue

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 AGI picture worries me most because my partner's bakery hours could change before robots touch our line crew, and then field robots arrive around 2031. I'd need the electricity company to publish a real staffing plan and pay for the testing course while we still have time.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Who gets to stop the work when the plan comes from software? A safe refusal has to count as doing the job, even when the street is dark. My apprenticeship taught me that a fast mistake is still a mistake. A safe refusal has to count as doing the lineworker's job, even when the street is dark.

headlineQuote: A safe refusal has to count as doing the lineworker's job, even when the street is dark.
portrait: **Bianca**, 43, repairs overhead electricity lines from South Road depot and values testing a wire before anyone climbs.
Her **mortgage**, two school-age children and three months of savings make her cautious despite fairly steady lineworker pay.
She uses AI **occasionally** for reports but wants field crews to challenge generated plans and supervise any repair robot.
In the fastest AGI picture, her partner's **bakery hours** may fall before robots threaten her own crew around 2031.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** threatens bakery hours before capable line-repair robots arrive around 2031, leaving the mortgage exposed.
whatWouldHelp: A published **staffing plan** and company-paid robotic line-testing course would let her prepare while still employed.
